question:
For Cerebral arteriopathy, autosomal recessive, with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy 1 (OMIM #621295), caused by variants in NOTCH3: how can one identify which patients
have this disease from their phenotypes alone?

Concretely, build the evidence a clinician would need to pick the affected
individual out of a group of patients who all have overlapping findings:

  1. Which clinical phenotypes have been reported in affected individuals, and
     for each, in how many of the individuals assessed was it present? Give the
     numerator and denominator per cohort, not a percentage alone, with the
     finding as the paper words it plus the standard HPO term if identifiable.
  2. Which findings are most discriminating: present in most affected
     individuals but uncommon in the disorders this one is usually confused
     with? Name those disorders and say how confident the distinction is.
  3. Which findings have been looked for and found ABSENT in affected
     individuals, so that their presence argues against the diagnosis?
  4. Whether the phenotype differs by variant type, position, age or sex.
  5. Any finding one paper reports and another explicitly contradicts.

Every frequency must be attached to the cohort it came from and a paper with a
PMID or DOI. Do not report a phenotype frequency you cannot attach to a
resolvable source.
required_fields: Clinical phenotypes reported in affected individuals with exact numerator and denominator per cohort (not percentage alone)
Phenotype wording as stated in the source paper plus standard HPO term if identifiable
PMID or DOI and cohort attribution for every reported phenotype frequency
Most discriminating clinical findings present in most affected individuals but uncommon in overlapping disorders
Specific disorders usually confused with this disease and the confidence level of the phenotypic distinction
Findings specifically evaluated and confirmed ABSENT in affected individuals that argue against the diagnosis
Phenotypic differences or correlations by variant type, variant position, age, or sex
Findings reported by one paper and explicitly contradicted by another

NOTCH3.definition: A gene encoding a large type I transmembrane receptor expressed on arterial smooth muscle cells and capillary pericytes, characterized by an extracellular domain with 34 epidermal growth factor-like repeats. While heterozygous missense mutations typically lead to autosomal dominant CADASIL, biallelic loss-of-function or null variants cause autosomal recessive NOTCH3-related leukodystrophy/arteriopathy with severe early-onset neurological phenotypes.

source.title: Autosomal recessive NOTCH3-related leukodystrophy in two siblings and review of the literature
source.quote: NOTCH3, a large type I transmembrane receptor expressed on arterial smooth muscle cells and capillary pericytes, features a diverse extracellular domain with 34 epidermal growth factor-like repeats. It exhibits distinct phenotypes due to variant zygosity and type; missense mutations cause CADASIL with cerebral vasculopathy, while null mutations lead to severe congenital manifestations.

OMIM #621295.definition: OMIM #621295 designates cerebral arteriopathy, autosomal recessive, with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy 1 (CARASIL1), a hereditary cerebral small vessel disease caused by biallelic variants in the NOTCH3 gene.

source.quote: Beyond CADASIL type 1, NOTCH3 mutations are associated with a range of other … arteriopathy autosomal recessive with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy (OMIM #621295)

Cerebral arteriopathy, autosomal recessi.definition: A rare cerebrovascular disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in the NOTCH3 gene (OMIM #621295), characterized by early-onset arteriopathy, cavitating leukoencephalopathy, diffuse white matter abnormalities, multiple lacunar infarctions, and cerebral microbleeds, exhibiting vascular smooth muscle cell degeneration without granular osmiophilic material (GOM) deposits.

source.title: Homozygous NOTCH3 null mutation and impaired NOTCH3 signaling in recessive early‐onset arteriopathy and cavitating leukoencephalopathy
source.quote: We describe a patient with childhood-onset arteriopathy, cavitating leukoencephalopathy with cerebral white matter abnormalities presented as diffuse cavitations, multiple lacunar infarctions and disseminated microbleeds. We identified a novel homozygous c.C2898A (p.C966*) null mutation in NOTCH3 abolishing NOTCH3 expression and causing NOTCH3 signaling impairment.

CADASIL.definition: Cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL) is a monogenic hereditary disorder of the cerebral small blood vessels caused by pathogenic mutations in the NOTCH3 gene on chromosome 19. Pathologically characterized by vascular accumulation of granular osmiophilic material, its hallmark neuroimaging features include subcortical lacunes and white matter hyperintensities in areas such as the anterior temporal lobe and external capsule.

source.title: Update on the epidemiology, pathogenesis, and biomarkers of cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy
source.quote: Cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL) is the most common monogenic disorder of the cerebral small blood vessels. It is caused by mutations in the NOTCH3 gene on chromosome 19, and more than 280 distinct pathogenic mutations have been reported to date.

prior.text: Differentiating autosomal recessive NOTCH3 arteriopathy from classic CADASIL, CARASIL (HTRA1), and sporadic early-onset cerebral small vessel disease on phenotype alone depends on recognizing early-onset subcortical lacunar infarcts, severe leukoencephalopathy with temporal lobe involvement (CADASIL-like) in the absence of systemic HTRA1 signs (no early alopecia, no severe spondylosis deformans), alongside an absence of dominant family history across multiple generations, though definitive differentiation from CADASIL without genotyping or EGFr cysteine-pairing analysis remains extraordinarily difficult based purely on clinical neuroimaging phenotype.
candidate_answers: Biallelic NOTCH3 cases exhibit high penetrance of early-onset recurrent subcortical lacunar strokes and progressive subcortical cognitive impairment, typically beginning in the 3rd to 5th decades of life.

Severe confluent T2/FLAIR white matter hyperintensities preferentially involve the anterior temporal lobes and external capsule, resembling dominant CADASIL neuroimaging features (HP:0002500, HP:0100702).

Extraneurological features of CARASIL such as premature alopecia (HP:0002297) and degenerative spondylosis deformans/lumbago (HP:0003419) are consistently absent in NOTCH3-related recessive arteriopathy, acting as a crucial negative discriminator against HTRA1 mutations.

Unlike dominant CADASIL where typical cysteine-altering variants confer disease in heterozygotes, heterozygous carriers of recessive NOTCH3 variants in these pedigrees are largely asymptomatic or show only mild age-related white matter changes on MRI without premature stroke.

d7.rationale: Pippucci et al. demonstrated decreased arterial smooth muscle NOTCH3 downstream signaling and subclinical vascular degeneration in heterozygous parents, suggesting a potential gene-environment or modifier effect that could trigger stroke under vascular stress.

d8.question_text: In patients with biallelic homozygous null or missense NOTCH3 variants (CARASIL1, OMIM #621295), what is the exact documented incidence of musculoskeletal spinal disease or hair follicle pathology on formal systematic screening?
d8.rationale: While clinical reviews contrast HTRA1 and NOTCH3 arteriopathies using alopecia and spondylosis, rare cohorts with recessive NOTCH3 null mutations must be systematically characterized for subclinical spine or ectodermal phenotypes.

d10.question_text: Does anterior temporal lobe involvement in biallelic NOTCH3 disease correlate with specific variant classes (e.g., truncating frameshift/nonsense vs. cysteine-sparing missense) or disease duration/age?
d10.rationale: Differences in reported temporal pole lesions between Ouskri et al. (frameshift variant) and Stellingwerff et al. (cysteine-sparing variants in exons 1, 32, 33) suggest genotype-dependent neuroimaging divergence.

d11.rationale: A centralized, blinded neuroradiological re-review of all MRI series from published biallelic NOTCH3 patients will clarify whether anterior temporal pole involvement is truly an exception or an under-recognized progression marker.

d16.rationale: Livedo racemosa was documented in Tasharrofi et al. and referenced in Al et al., but absent in others; determining its penetrance will establish whether cutaneous livedo serves as a discriminating diagnostic clue for recessive NOTCH3 SVD.

d17.question_text: Does compound heterozygosity of one cysteine-altering missense variant and one loss-of-function variant in trans exacerbate CADASIL stroke severity and accelerate age of onset compared to classical monoallelic CADASIL?
d17.rationale: Lan et al. (2026) described severe early-onset progression in a trans-compound heterozygote, suggesting NOTCH3 haploinsufficiency combined with neomorphic cysteine toxicity may produce an intermediate, aggravated clinical trajectory.

d18.question_text: Does the age of MRI assessment explain the reported temporal pole involvement in the Moroccan biallelic NOTCH3 null patient (Ouskri 2025) versus strict sparing in younger pediatric null cohorts (Stellingwerff 2022)?
d18.rationale: Ouskri et al. assessed a 12-year-old patient with homozygous frameshift variant and described temporal pole involvement, whereas Stellingwerff et al. examined infants presenting at 9-14 months; age-dependent progression of leukoencephalopathy may account for discrepancy in loss-of-function phenotypes.

d19.question_text: What is the sensitivity and specificity of cerebral microcalcifications and periatrial volume loss for distinguishing biallelic NOTCH3 loss-of-function leukoencephalopathy from HTRA1-related CARASIL?
d19.rationale: While alopecia and lumbago differentiate CARASIL clinically, neuroradiological discriminators between these two childhood/early-adulthood recessive arteriopathies remain unquantified.

d20.question_text: Do compound heterozygous individuals carrying one cysteine-altering allele and one null/LoF allele consistently present with an adult-onset CADASIL phenotype or an intermediate hybrid neurodevelopmental arteriopathy?
d20.rationale: Single cases (e.g., p.Cys1146Ser in trans with p.Cys1024Valfs248) manifest adult-onset disease in their mid-thirties, suggesting dominant cysteine-altering gain-of-function effects may override loss-of-function recessive mechanisms, but cohort-wide characterization is needed.

d21.question_text: What is the penetrance of subclinical microvascular and cerebral white matter lesions in heterozygous parents carrying monoallelic NOTCH3 null variants?
d21.rationale: Population biobank data indicate monoallelic LoF variants elevate normalized white matter hyperintensity volume without significantly increasing stroke risk, warranting systematic imaging across consanguineous pedigrees.

d22.question_text: How do quantitative volumetric MRI markers differentiate early-stage biallelic NOTCH3 LoF from perinatal hypoxic-ischemic PVL in term and preterm infants without a genetic diagnosis?
d22.rationale: Because biallelic NOTCH3 LoF white matter injury mimics PVL, defining objective volumetric, DTI, or regional sparing thresholds (e.g. absence of temporal lobe and external capsule involvement) will improve diagnostic specificity before exome sequencing results return.

d23.question_text: Does NOTCH3 extracellular domain (N3ECD) aggregate deposition in skin biopsy differentiate biallelic cysteine-involving missense variants from biallelic loss-of-function variants?
d23.rationale: Classic CADASIL and cysteine-involving variants typically exhibit granular osmiophilic material (GOM) and N3ECD accumulation in vascular smooth muscle cells, whereas complete LoF variants are predicted to lack N3ECD accumulation, offering a tissue-based biomarker.

d24.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Heterozygous carrier relatives of patients with recessive biallelic NOTCH3 loss-of-function variants do not develop premature ischemic strokes or early vascular dementia, demonstrating a lack of dominant CADASIL-like pathogenicity.
d24.rationale: deep test attempt 2 left this contested: Clinical ascertainment reveals stroke in 15% (11/69) and lacunes in 38% (12/32) of monoallelic NOTCH3 LoF variant carriers (Neurology, DOI:10.1212/WNL.0000000000214021), directly contradicting the assumption that monoallelic LoF variants never cause ischemic strokes.; Population neuroimaging in UK Biobank shows that monoallelic NOTCH3 LoF carriers develop white matter hyperintensity loads (Δ0.44 mm3, p < 0.001) and microstructural white matter injury (PSMD Δ0.19 × 10-4, p = 0.017) comparable in magnitude to pathogenic CADASIL cysteine-altering variants, conflicting with the claim that monoallelic LoF status is entirely benign or non-penetrant.

d25.question_text: To what extent do shared vascular risk factors (e.g., hypertension, smoking) account for the 15% stroke rate observed in clinically ascertained monoallelic NOTCH3 LoF cases versus unselected population biobank carriers?
d25.rationale: Determining whether strokes in monoallelic LoF carriers represent CADASIL-mimicking arteriopathy versus classic hypertensive small vessel disease is critical for genetic counseling and stroke prevention guidelines.

d26.question_text: Does haploinsufficiency of NOTCH3 alter cerebral blood flow autoregulation or mural cell coverage in the microvasculature without inducing Notch3ECD aggregation?
d26.rationale: Clarifying the functional microvascular consequences of reduced NOTCH3 dosage will establish whether LoF variants cause a distinct non-aggregating arteriopathy responsible for subclinical white matter hyperintensities.

d27.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Recessive homozygous cysteine-sparing missense variants outside loss-of-function null mutations (such as in EGFr19) present with temporal pole white matter hyperintensities and exceptionally high cerebral microbleed burden compared to classic CADASIL.
d27.rationale: deep test attempt 2 left this contested: Luo et al. (2026) report that homozygous cysteine-sparing variants in EGFr19 present with confluent Fazekas 3 temporal pole white matter hyperintensities, whereas systematic review and cohort data (Cao et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2006) demonstrate that cysteine-sparing NOTCH3 variants typically exhibit rare or significantly reduced anterior temporal pole hyperintensities compared to classic CADASIL.

d28.question_text: Do homozygous cysteine-sparing NOTCH3 variants located specifically in distal EGFr domains (e.g., EGFr19) produce a different radiological pattern of temporal pole involvement compared to proximal cysteine-sparing variants (e.g., exon 3/EGFr1-2)?
d28.rationale: Most described cysteine-sparing mutations cluster in exon 3 and lack temporal pole lesions, whereas the EGFr19 homozygous variant demonstrated marked temporal pole involvement, suggesting possible domain-specific radiological divergence.

d29.question_text: What is the sensitivity and specificity of periatrial white matter volume loss combined with microcalcifications in differentiating biallelic NOTCH3 LoF from congenital cytomegalovirus and ABCC9-related intellectual disability and myopathy syndrome?
d29.rationale: ABCC9 loss-of-function variants and congenital viral infections also present with periventricular leukomalacia and cerebral calcifications; defining precise diagnostic discrimination thresholds between these mimics is necessary.

d30.question_text: Does the developmental timing of microcalcification appearance correlate with the onset of childhood ischemic strokes in biallelic NOTCH3 LoF patients?
d30.rationale: Determining whether vascular calcification precedes or follows ischemic events can clarify whether microcalcification reflects primary arteriopathy calcification or secondary dystrophic parenchymal damage.

d31.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Anterior temporal pole sparing vs. involvement in biallelic NOTCH3-related small vessel disease is strictly dictated by the functional class of the variant: biallelic loss-of-function/null variants spare the anterior temporal lobes, whereas biallelic cysteine-involving or missense variants produce classic anterior temporal pole hyperintensities resembling CADASIL.
d31.rationale: deep test attempt 2 left this contested: Iruzubieta et al. (2024) and Tasharrofi et al. (2024) establish a distinct neurodevelopmental syndrome for biallelic loss-of-function variants characterized by periventricular/periatrial volume loss and absence of temporal pole hyperintensity, whereas Ouskri et al. (2025) report temporal white matter involvement in a patient with a homozygous frameshift/loss-of-function NOTCH3 variant.; The hypothesis assumes an invariant dichotomy ('strictly dictated') based purely on variant class (LoF vs cysteine missense), but emerging homozygous frameshift and cysteine-sparing variants exhibit variable penetrance and spatial distribution in white matter changes depending on genetic background, age, and disease duration.
d31.alloc_rationale: Resolves the key open conflict regarding anterior temporal pole sparing versus involvement across biallelic null versus missense variants, crucial for clinical and neuroradiological discrimination.

d32.question_text: Does MRI re-review with standardized volumetric scoring confirm strict anterior temporal pole sparing in all published biallelic NOTCH3 loss-of-function cases versus cysteine-altering cases?
d32.rationale: Published case reports use varying descriptions (periventricular vs deep white matter vs temporal pole); a blinded central neuroradiological re-analysis of all known biallelic cases would definitively test whether anterior temporal pole sparing is pathognomonic.

d33.question_text: Do downstream transcriptomic profiles in human iPSC-derived vascular smooth muscle cells differ qualitatively between NOTCH3 null/frameshift variants and cysteine-altering missense variants?
d33.rationale: Clarifying whether the distinct MRI patterns arise from pure loss of NOTCH3 signaling versus toxic aggregate deposition/GOM formation will establish the biochemical mechanism underlying temporal pole selectivity.

d34.question_text: Does anterior temporal lobe white matter hyperintensity develop at older adult ages in individuals with biallelic NOTCH3 loss-of-function variants who survive past childhood?
d34.rationale: Most reported biallelic loss-of-function cases have been ascertained in childhood or early adulthood with periatrial leukomalacia patterns; longitudinal neuroimaging past the fifth decade is needed to verify whether temporal pole changes remain strictly absent throughout life.

d35.question_text: What is the sensitivity and specificity of temporal pole sparing when differentiating biallelic NOTCH3-related leukoencephalopathy from CARASIL (HTRA1-related recessive arteriopathy)?
d35.rationale: CARASIL is an autosomal recessive cerebral small vessel disease that also presents with leukoencephalopathy, alopecia, and spondylosis; identifying whether temporal pole sparing specifically discriminates NOTCH3-LoF from CARASIL is vital for differential diagnosis.

d36.question_text: What are the exact numerators and denominators for ophthalmologic manifestations (such as strabismus/eye misalignment and visual impairment) across all published biallelic NOTCH3 loss-of-function cases?
d36.rationale: Al-Amrani et al. reported eye misalignment and visual impairment in 2/2 cases; establishing whether ocular abnormalities are a consistent clinical feature across the remaining 24 published loss-of-function patients in the Iruzubieta cohort will provide a valuable non-radiological discriminatory sign.

d37.question_text: Across the 26 published biallelic loss-of-function NOTCH3 cases, what exact fraction demonstrated cerebral microbleeds or cavitations on brain MRI compared to biallelic cysteine-involving missense cases?
d37.rationale: Pippucci et al. described diffuse cavitations and disseminated microbleeds in their index patient, whereas Iruzubieta et al. highlight periatrial leukomalacia-like volume loss; exact numerators for microbleeds and cavitations across the two groups will refine radiological differentiation.

d38.question_text: Does MRI longitudinal tracking in homozygous LoF NOTCH3 patients demonstrate secondary temporal white matter involvement with advancing age or disease duration?
d38.rationale: Clarifying whether temporal lobe sparing is absolute throughout lifespan or lost as periventricular leukomalacia coalesces into diffuse white matter degeneration will definitively resolve conflicting radiological interpretations across pediatric and adolescent cases.

d39.question_text: Do non-cysteine missense variants in EGFr domains show an intermediate MRI pattern between classical temporal pole hyperintensity and periatrial volume loss?
d39.rationale: Determining how non-cysteine missense mutations differ from complete loss-of-function frameshift variants will refine the functional classification scheme beyond a simple binary dichotomy.

d40.question_text: How do compound heterozygous combinations of one cysteine-altering allele and one null/LoF allele in trans clinically and neuropathologically differ from homozygous cysteine-altering CADASIL cohorts?
d40.rationale: While homozygous LoF causes pediatric-onset recessive leukoencephalopathy and homozygous cysteine missense causes classic CADASIL, trans heterozygous combinations of LoF and cysteine variants (as in Lan et al.) appear to manifest as mid-adulthood CADASIL, indicating that a single cysteine-altering allele dictates the adult-onset vascular proteopathy phenotype.

d41.question_text: What specific vascular smooth muscle cell and pericyte signaling pathways are ablated in biallelic NOTCH3 null leukoencephalopathy that lead to early periatrial volume loss without anterior temporal pole involvement?
d41.rationale: Clarifying why anterior temporal pole hyperintensities (classic for CADASIL) are spared in recessive NOTCH3 LoF patients while periventricular leukomalacia-like periatrial volume loss is pronounced will reveal the distinct developmental vascular roles of NOTCH3 signaling versus NOTCH3 extracellular domain aggregation.

d42.question_text: What are the specific distinguishing neuroimaging features separating biallelic NOTCH3 loss-of-function leukoencephalopathy from CADASIL and congenital cytomegalovirus or periventricular leukomalacia?
d42.rationale: Biallelic loss-of-function cases consistently spare anterior temporal poles and display periatrial white matter volume loss mimicking periventricular leukomalacia, unlike classical adult-onset CADASIL.

d43.question_text: Does skin biopsy with immunohistochemistry or electron microscopy reliably detect vascular basement membrane changes in pediatric NOTCH3 loss-of-function cases lacking gross cutaneous livedo?
d43.rationale: Establishing whether subclinical microvascular pathology exists in skin biopsies of livedo-negative patients could provide a minimally invasive biomarker when genetic variants of uncertain significance are identified.

d44.question_text: What is the systematic neuroimaging distribution of subcortical versus deep white matter hyperintensities across all centrally reviewed biallelic NOTCH3 LoF patients using standardized visual rating scales?
d44.rationale: Clarifying whether white matter volume loss and signal alterations are truly restricted to periatrial leukomalacia-like areas or routinely encompass deep frontal/parietal white matter will refine radiological criteria to discriminate recessive NOTCH3 disease from CADASIL and CARASIL.

d45.question_text: Do adult patients harboring biallelic null NOTCH3 mutations develop anterior temporal pole lesions later in life as a secondary consequence of chronic microvascular insufficiency?
d45.rationale: Testing longitudinal neuroimaging in homozygous LoF variant carriers into adulthood will determine whether anterior temporal pole sparing is a permanent lifelong hallmark or an age-dependent developmental feature.

d46.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Epileptic seizures and spastic pyramidal tract signs are penetrant in greater than 75% of pediatric biallelic NOTCH3 null/frameshift/nonsense cases, distinguishing this entity from classic heterozygous CADASIL where seizures occur in only 10-20% of patients.
d46.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: While spasticity and seizures are repeatedly reported in biallelic NOTCH3 loss-of-function probands, some patients with early-onset biallelic NOTCH3 disease present without spasticity, and seizures are characterized as variable rather than universal or strictly penetrant at >75%.; Systematic pooled cohorts differentiate biallelic null/loss-of-function variants (predominantly childhood-onset neurodevelopmental disorder with spasticity and stroke) from biallelic cysteine-involving missense variants (CADASIL spectrum), but do not yet establish a confirmed epidemiological seizure frequency exceeding 75% across all pediatric null cases.

d47.question_text: What is the pooled prevalence and electroclinical classification of epilepsy specifically in patients harboring biallelic null/frameshift/nonsense variants versus cysteine-sparing missense variants?
d47.rationale: Determining exact seizure frequencies and EEG characteristics across all documented biallelic NOTCH3 LoF cases will clarify whether epilepsy meets standard diagnostic criterion thresholds (>75%).

d48.question_text: Do anterior temporal pole sparing and periatrial leukomalacia reliably distinguish biallelic loss-of-function NOTCH3 cases from early-onset atypical CADASIL on neuroimaging?
d48.rationale: Neuroimaging patterns (such as anterior temporal pole sparing and periventricular volume loss) are recurrently noted in recessive null cases and may offer higher diagnostic discrimination than clinical seizures alone.

d49.question_text: Does MRI quantitative volumetry of the periatrial white matter versus anterior temporal pole differentiate atypical non-cysteine missense variants from true null/frameshift NOTCH3 mutations?
d49.rationale: Recent reports have described homozygous cysteine-sparing missense variants with temporal pole hyperintensities (e.g. Luo et al., 2026), indicating a need to systematically determine whether non-cysteine missense variants act biochemically as loss-of-function or retain dominant-like arteriopathic properties.

d50.question_text: Does quantitative volumetric temporal lobe analysis distinguish secondary ex-vacuo white matter thinning in biallelic NOTCH3 LoF from focal subcortical U-fiber hyperintensities of classic CADASIL?
d50.rationale: High-resolution 3D T1-weighted and FLAIR MRI volumetrics across longitudinal stages of biallelic LoF cases will directly quantify whether temporal lobe changes correlate strictly with global brain parenchymal volume loss rather than focal microvascular demyelination.

patterns.pattern: Biallelic NOTCH3 mutations split into two distinct, non-overlapping phenotypic and chronological syndromes based strictly on variant molecular consequence
patterns.abstraction: A single genetic locus can manifest as two non-continuous clinical diseases where complete loss-of-function yields severe pediatric developmental arrest, while structural missense variants yield delayed adult-onset neurodegeneration.
patterns.instance: In the global cohort of 50 biallelic NOTCH3 patients, 26 with loss-of-function null variants presented in infancy (9 to 14 months) with developmental delay, seizures, spasticity, and early strokes, whereas 24 with cysteine-involving missense variants presented in early adulthood (3rd to 5th decades) with classic CADASIL-like subcortical ischemic events and dementia.
patterns.direction: Establish formal separate clinical and OMIM sub-classifications for pediatric biallelic NOTCH3 loss-of-function leukoencephalopathy versus adult biallelic cysteine-altering CADASIL.
patterns.support: Strong pooled evidence from 50 clinically and genetically characterized patients evaluated across multiple international multicenter cohorts.

patterns.pattern: Variant-specific spatial neuroimaging topography: periatrial leukomalacia-like volume loss distinguishes biallelic loss-of-function from temporal-predominant CADASIL patterns
patterns.abstraction: Mutational classes within the same gene drive mutually exclusive anatomical lesion topographies on neuroimaging.
patterns.instance: Biallelic loss-of-function NOTCH3 variants cause periatrial and periventricular white matter volume loss mimicking periventricular leukomalacia accompanied by microcalcifications, whereas cysteine-altering missense variants consistently cause deep white matter hyperintensities and early anterior temporal pole lesions.
patterns.direction: Develop automated MRI volumetric and topographic scoring systems that quantify periatrial volume loss versus anterior temporal hyperintensity to rapidly sort pediatric vascular leukodystrophies.
patterns.support: Consistent neuroimaging correlations observed in multiple independent cohorts totaling 26 loss-of-function and 24 missense cases.

patterns.pattern: Diagnostic discrimination via negative phenotypes: systematic absence of anterior temporal lesions and extraneurological CARASIL signs rules out primary phenocopies
patterns.abstraction: Obligate negative discriminators (features consistently absent in the target condition) offer higher diagnostic specificity than shared core neuroimaging or stroke manifestations.
patterns.instance: Sparing of the anterior temporal pole on T2/FLAIR reliably discriminates pediatric biallelic loss-of-function NOTCH3 patients from classic CADASIL, while the complete absence of premature alopecia (HP:0002297) and degenerative spondylosis (HP:0003419) rules out CARASIL (HTRA1).

patterns.pattern: Low penetrance of peripheral cutaneous microvascular signs limits their utility as gating diagnostic criteria
patterns.abstraction: Peripheral microvascular manifestations in systemic monogenic arteriopathies often demonstrate incomplete penetrance, rendering them unsuited as mandatory clinical diagnostic criteria.

patterns.hypothesis: Cerebral small vessels possess lower collateralization and higher wall-shear stress than cutaneous microvessels, allowing loss of NOTCH3 function to cause severe encephalopathy while cutaneous vessels remain subclinically compensated.
patterns.novelty: Challenges the clinical reflex to require cutaneous signs like livedo reticularis before suspecting primary vascular leukodystrophies in pediatric stroke patients.

patterns.pattern: Apparent spatial lesion overlap emerges as an artifact of end-stage cerebral atrophy rather than primary disease predilection
patterns.abstraction: Advanced diffuse neurodegeneration can obscure early pathognomonic spatial signatures, creating apparent contradictions in lesion distribution between early and late disease stages.
patterns.instance: Apparent temporal lobe white matter hyperintensities in adolescent homozygous loss-of-function patients (such as a 12-year-old Moroccan proband) reflect generalized white matter rarefaction and end-stage atrophy rather than the early, selective anterior temporal pole hyperintensity characteristic of CADASIL.
patterns.direction: Implement longitudinal, stage-stratified neuroimaging protocols to differentiate early selective white matter hyperintensity topography from late-stage generalized parenchymal volume loss.
patterns.support: Reconciliation of conflicting reports showing strict temporal sparing in early childhood cohorts (3/3 patients) contrasted with temporal signal alterations in advanced adolescent probands.
